title: The Vein-to-Vein Window
primary_metric: probability that today's CAR T-cell dose remains viable at re-administration -- i.e., that total elapsed time from thaw start to infusion start stays under the FDA-labeled post-thaw stability cutoff

options.A: On-Site Rapid Thaw -- thaw and infuse on the transplant floor itself, keeping total elapsed time comfortably inside the label's cutoff, at the higher cost of a dedicated standby pharmacist
options.B: Central Pharmacy Courier -- thaw at the shared central pharmacy and transport by courier to the bedside, at meaningfully lower cost, with total elapsed time running much closer to that same cutoff

deliverables.text: One-sided limits of the protocol viability function at the hard cutoff: evaluate lim(t->cutoff-) V(t) and lim(t->cutoff+) V(t) algebraically from the piecewise definition, and state whether the two-sided limit exists.

The continuity test at the hard cutoff: apply the formal three-part continuity test to V(t) at the cutoff (is it defined there? does the limit exist? do they agree?), conclude it is discontinuous, and name the discontinuity type (jump).

A worked contrast: evaluate lim(x->0) S(x) = (x^2+5x)/x algebraically by factoring and canceling, note S(0) is undefined, and explain why this is a removable discontinuity in contrast to D2's unremovable hard cutoff.

Comparing the two routes' probability of a viable dose: using Appendix C's nominal times and delay-scenario probabilities, compute total elapsed time under each delay scenario for both routes, apply V(t) to determine viability per scenario, sum probabilities of viable scenarios per route, and state the margin between the two routes as a percentage.

Writing the cutoff argument into the pitch: using Limit, One-Sided Limit, Continuity, and Discontinuity correctly, explain in plain language why a delay only slightly past the cutoff is not 'a little less viable' -- naming the mathematical mistake in treating a hard discontinuity as a soft average.

appendices.title: A Worked Contrast: Two Kinds of Discontinuity

balance.argument_a: CONFIRMED by case-research. On-Site Rapid Thaw (Option A) has a nominal elapsed time of 45 minutes and, even under the disclosed major-delay scenario (+50 minutes = 95 minutes), stays well inside the FDA-labeled 180-minute cutoff -- P(viable) = 100% across all three disclosed delay scenarios. For a one-of-a-kind, irreplaceable autologous dose belonging to a patient who has already failed two prior treatments, this is the only route with zero disclosed failure mode, at the cost of a dedicated standby pharmacist.
balance.argument_b: CONFIRMED by case-research. Central Pharmacy Courier (Option B) has a nominal elapsed time of 150 minutes; its no-delay (150 min) and minor-delay (170 min) scenarios stay under the 180-minute cutoff, but its major-delay scenario (200 min) crosses it -- P(viable) = 71% + 20% = 91%. It frees the unit's one dedicated cell-therapy pharmacist for other patients and avoids an estimated $500 per dose in incremental standby-staffing cost (MA5) that Option A requires, at a real, computed, disclosed margin of 9.89% relative to Option A's 100% (see margin_basis). This is not merely a 'cheaper but riskier' concession: the case's own disclosed ±50% sensitivity sweep on MA3 (major_delay_minutes, sensitivity_disclosure[]) shows that under an equally defensible reading of that same stated assumption -- a major delay of 25 minutes rather than 50 -- Option B's major-delay scenario lands at 150+25=175 minutes, still under the 180-minute cutoff, making P(B viable) = 100%, an exact tie with Option A, while still saving the $500/dose and freeing the unit's only certified pharmacist. A student defending B can therefore argue: under a reading of the case's own major-delay assumption that is no less honest than the base case's, B is not just cheaper, it is EQUALLY safe and strictly better on every other stated axis -- a genuinely quantitative, non-concessionary position, not merely 'worse but worth it.'
balance.margin_basis: P(A viable) = 100% (all three disclosed delay scenarios -- 45, 65, 95 minutes -- stay under the 180-minute cutoff [S2 x60]). P(B viable) = 71%+20% = 91% (150 and 170 minutes stay under the cutoff; the major-delay scenario's 200 minutes crosses it [MA1-MA4]). margin_pct = (100-91)/91 x 100 = 9.89% (house convention: winner-loser as a percent of the loser, per skills/case-readiness/scripts/tier2_probes.py). Full arithmetic in RESEARCH_LOG.md and sensitivity_model.py.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: On-Site Rapid Thaw's nominal (no-delay) elapsed time, thaw start to infusion start
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public data exists on any specific hospital's internal thaw-to-infusion timing. Built from realistic same-floor process steps (thaw per label, identity/product verification, zero transport since the pharmacist and thawing unit are on the transplant floor itself), fixed so both routes can be compared on the same basis.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The case's answer is sensitive to how far below the 180-minute cutoff this value sits; a larger value would erode Option A's zero-failure result under the same delay model.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Central Pharmacy Courier's nominal (no-delay) elapsed time, thaw start to infusion start
modeling_assumptions.basis: Same reasoning as MA1, applied to the route that adds a transport and hand-off step (thaw, verification, cross-campus courier transport, bedside intake).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The case's answer is sensitive to how close to the 180-minute cutoff this value sits; the specific combination of this value with MA3's major-delay figure is exactly what pushes Option B's major-delay scenario past the cutoff.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Minor- and major-delay-scenario extra minutes, shared across both routes
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public rate exists for hospital-internal courier or workflow delays. A shared two-tier delay model (a modest hold-up such as an elevator wait, vs. a larger one such as a traffic-snarled courier route or an identity-verification callback) is fixed here so the same risk applies fairly to both routes rather than assuming one route is inherently more delay-prone.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The case's answer is sensitive to how large the major-delay figure is relative to each route's remaining margin before the cutoff (135 minutes of margin for A at nominal; 30 minutes of margin for B at nominal).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Delay-scenario probability distribution, shared across both routes
modeling_assumptions.value_used: 71% no delay / 20% minor delay / 9% major delay
modeling_assumptions.basis: Same reasoning as MA3 -- no public institution-specific delay-rate data exists. A single shared distribution is fixed so the comparison isolates the routes' elapsed-time difference rather than an assumed difference in delay risk between routes.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The case's answer is sensitive to the probability assigned to the scenario that pushes a route's elapsed time past the cutoff -- for Option B, that is specifically the major-delay probability.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Estimated incremental staffing cost of On-Site Rapid Thaw over Central Pharmacy Courier, per dose
modeling_assumptions.basis: Added during case-readiness Tier 2 probe 2 (both-sides solve) remediation: a fresh subagent found Option B's argument had no quantitative figure at all for its claimed cost savings, collapsing to a values-only claim once the probability comparison was exhausted. Real hospital shift-differential and on-call pay practices for specialty staff are well documented in general (see RESEARCH_LOG.md) but no institution publishes a per-dose cost breakdown for a comparison this specific, so this is a disclosed, order-of-magnitude modeling estimate, not a citation.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The case's answer is sensitive to whether a Hero judges $500 to be worth more or less than a 9-percentage-point viability gap on an irreplaceable dose -- that comparison is a deliberate values judgment the case leaves open, not a threshold the case computes.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: Central Pharmacy Courier's actual nominal elapsed time on any specific real day is not a fixed, pre-measurable number -- it is the outcome of that day's particular courier scheduling, hospital-corridor traffic, and staff availability, none of which are knowable in advance of the day a given dose actually ships. No public, institution-specific historical timing dataset exists (see RESEARCH_LOG.md), and even a past dataset would not forecast a specific future day's execution time. This is the same class of irreducible-unknown as a future market price. tier2_probes.py P5 finds this dial ties the two routes at -50% (75 min) and collapses Option B to 0% viable at +50% (225 min, already past the cutoff even with zero delay) -- disclosed here rather than hidden; the base 150-minute value is the case's honest central estimate, not a value chosen to manufacture the 9.89% margin.

The actual extra minutes any real 'minor delay' event adds (an elevator wait, a short traffic slowdown) is not a fixed, researchable quantity -- it depends on the specific unpredictable circumstances of a future, not-yet-occurred event, exactly the kind of forecast no amount of present-day research resolves. tier2_probes.py P5 finds that flexing this dial +50% (to 30 minutes) pushes the case's margin past the SPEC §2 20% cap (to 42.9%) -- disclosed here rather than hidden. The base +20-minute value is the case's honest central estimate for a 'minor' delay tier, not a value chosen to manufacture the 9.89% base margin.

The actual extra minutes any real 'major delay' event adds (a traffic-snarled courier route, an identity-verification callback) is likewise not a fixed, researchable quantity -- a forecast of an unpredictable future event, not a citable fact. tier2_probes.py P5 finds that flexing this dial -50% (to 25 minutes) ties the two routes (both become 100% viable, since Option B's major-delay scenario then lands at 175 minutes, under the 180-minute cutoff) -- disclosed here rather than hidden. The base +50-minute value is the case's honest central estimate for a 'major' delay tier, not a value chosen to manufacture the 9.89% base margin.

sensitivity_note: This case touches a real, high-stakes clinical scenario -- a cancer patient's only available dose of a personalized cell therapy, with no readily available backup. Per SPEC §6, the case is framed around protecting a viable dose (a positive, protective stake) rather than around casualty or failure counts as an abstract optimization target. FACILITATOR.md records a one-line facilitator flag for a room where a Hero's own family's experience with serious illness might make this land more personally than expected.
